slots.practicalActivity: Pick three real Power BI tenant settings you'd expect to exist (e.g. export data, publish to web, external sharing) and for each one write who in a hypothetical organization should be allowed to toggle it and why. Then assign the four workspace roles (Admin, Member, Contributor, Viewer) to four named people on a hypothetical finance reporting team, justifying each assignment in one sentence.
slots.deliverable: Three tenant-setting ownership decisions with reasoning, plus a four-role workspace assignment for a named team.

slots.practicalActivity: For a company with three departments (finance, sales, operations) each needing their own reports but sharing one semantic model, decide between a per-department workspace pattern and a shared workspace pattern, with one sentence justifying your choice. Then sketch the Power BI app you'd publish from it: its name, which workspace content it includes, and which audience (by security group) gets access.
slots.deliverable: A justified workspace-pattern decision for a three-department scenario, plus a sketched app with its audience.

slots.practicalActivity: Tenant and workspace lab: design a complete workspace structure for a hypothetical five-person BI team supporting two departments. Name each workspace, its role assignments (who is Admin/Member/Contributor/Viewer), one tenant setting you'd restrict for this team, and the one app you'd publish for end-user consumption.
slots.deliverable: A full workspace structure document: named workspaces, role assignments, one restricted tenant setting, and one published app definition.

slots.practicalActivity: For a sales semantic model, write the DAX filter expression you'd use to define two RLS roles (Eastern US and Western US) in Power BI Desktop's Manage roles dialog. Then describe the Object Level Security setting (Default, Read, or None) you'd apply to a Cost column so the Western US role can never even see that the column exists, and name one visual or measure risk you'd have to audit before publishing that change.
slots.deliverable: Two RLS DAX filter expressions for named roles, plus an OLS setting decision for a sensitive column with its audit risk noted.

slots.practicalActivity: Decide, for the same sales semantic model, whether to share it via direct report sharing or via Build permission on the dataset, with one sentence justifying the choice for an analyst who needs to build new reports on top of it. Then assign a Microsoft Purview sensitivity label (e.g. Confidential) to the model and name one downstream behavior that label change should trigger (export restriction, encryption, or visual watermark).
slots.deliverable: A sharing-method decision with justification, plus a sensitivity-label assignment and one triggered downstream behavior.

slots.practicalActivity: RLS/OLS lab: using the two RLS roles from the earlier slot, use (or describe) 'Test as role' to confirm what a user in the Eastern US role actually sees, then confirm what happens when a user is accidentally added to both roles (RLS applies the union of matching filters). Separately, using Tabular Editor's Object Level Security property, set a Cost column to None for the Western US role and describe what happens to a report visual that still references it.
slots.deliverable: A tested RLS result for a single-role and a dual-role user, plus an OLS None setting with its visual-breakage consequence described.

lessons.title: Lineage and Impact Analysis in Power BI

slots.practicalActivity: Pick three reports or datasets you use regularly (your own org's, or ones described in this course). For each, decide which endorsement level it should carry -- None, Promoted, or Certified -- and justify the call in one sentence, noting which one would need an admin-granted certifier permission before you could set it. Then describe the lineage view you'd open before changing a column in your most-used dataset, and name one downstream report that impact analysis should surface.
slots.deliverable: Three justified endorsement-level decisions, plus a lineage-based impact-analysis check before a hypothetical column change.

slots.practicalActivity: Design a usage-metrics review: name the one Usage Metrics report tile you'd check monthly to find reports nobody is viewing (candidates for deprecation), and the one you'd check to find which certified datasets are most relied upon. Then describe the Power BI Activity Log or Microsoft Purview audit query you'd run to answer 'who exported data from this specific certified dataset in the last 30 days.'
slots.deliverable: Two named usage-metrics checks with their purpose, plus one described audit query answering a real export-tracking question.

slots.practicalActivity: Trust and quality lab: for a semantic model you've designed earlier in this course, write the full trust case -- its endorsement level with justification, the lineage path you'd check before a breaking change, one usage-metrics signal that would justify deprecating it, and one audit-log question a compliance reviewer might ask about who accessed it.
slots.deliverable: A written trust case for one semantic model covering endorsement, lineage, usage signals, and an audit question.

slots.practicalActivity: Sketch the three-stage deployment pipeline (Development, Test, Production) you'd set up for the sales semantic model from earlier in this course. Name each stage's backing workspace, and write one sentence per stage describing who should be allowed to assign or unassign a workspace to it -- noting how that answer gets stricter moving toward Production. Then name one enterprise-wide governance control (a certification policy, a tenant setting, or a sensitivity-label rule) that should apply identically across all three stages.
slots.deliverable: A named three-stage pipeline with per-stage access rules, plus one enterprise governance control applied consistently across stages.

slots.practicalActivity: Work through the course's case study, naming the specific governance gap the fictional organization has at each stage (workspace sprawl, missing RLS, no endorsement standard, no deployment pipeline). Then complete the course's own practice lab exercise end to end, tracking which tasks you completed without looking back at earlier lessons.
slots.deliverable: A gap analysis of the course case study by governance area, plus a completed run of the course's practice lab.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone review: write a one-to-two-page Power BI governance plan for a hypothetical mid-size organization. Cover the workspace structure and role assignments, one RLS and one OLS control on a real semantic model, an endorsement standard (who can Certify and under what criteria), a three-stage deployment pipeline with per-stage access rules, and one usage-metrics or audit check you'd run monthly.
slots.deliverable: A one-to-two-page written Power BI governance plan covering workspace structure, model security, trust standards, lifecycle pipeline, and an ongoing audit check.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can design a Power BI workspace and tenant-settings structure, configure row-level and object-level security on a real semantic model, apply and justify endorsement levels, build and govern a three-stage deployment pipeline, and read usage metrics and audit logs to prove governance controls are working -- the full hands-on Power BI governance skillset the Data Governance Engineer path assumes a student can execute end to end.
